Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • 01Define and explain the concept of suitability analysis within the context of Geographic Information Systems (GIS).
  • 02Describe the significance of suitability analysis in spatial decision-making.
  • 03Explain the interrelationship between criteria, constraints, and the geographic space in suitability analysis.
  • 04Understand the role of weights in influencing the outcomes of a suitability analysis.
  • 05Work with the essential tools and software used for conducting suitability analysis in ArcGIS.
  • 06Execute the sequential steps in a suitability analysis, including preprocessing, weighting, and final evaluation.
  • 07Interpret the results of a suitability analysis.

Multi-criteria evaluation / analysis (MCE / MCA)

Multi-criteria evaluation (MCE) is a structured approach to evaluating multiple options when making a decision.

Why is it used? Complex decisions often require balancing trade-offs with multiple stakeholders.

Goal: evaluate whether each option meets certain criteria and, based on this, give each option an overall ranking.

What is suitability analysis?

Suitability analysis is a spatial approach to multi-criteria evaluation and analysis (MCE/MCA). It helps us qualify, compare, and rank candidate locations based on how well they meet a set of criteria that we define for a particular goal.

In GIS, it provides a transparent and systematic way to support location-based decision-making, such as choosing land for conservation, urban development, emergency facilities, or commercial uses.

A simple way to think about it: if decision-making in everyday life involves comparing options based on several preferences, then suitability analysis does the same thing for places. Instead of comparing houses, jobs, or phones, we compare map locations.

Why do we use suitability analysis?

Many real-world spatial decisions involve trade-offs. A location may be:

  • ·Close to roads, but too steep
  • ·Inexpensive, but environmentally sensitive
  • ·Ideal for one stakeholder and poor for another

Suitability analysis gives us a framework for making those trade-offs explicit. This is especially useful when there are multiple criteria, the criteria do not use the same units, some criteria are more important than others, some areas must be excluded entirely, and decision-makers want a process that is systematic and explainable.

Common applications

Suitability analysis is used across many fields. Examples include habitat suitability, cropland evaluation, landfill siting, solar and wind farm siting, urban development, micromobility planning, emergency shelter siting, and conservation planning.

The overall workflow

Cartographic models combine spatial layers via overlay, buffers, reclassification, and other spatial operations. One example of a cartographic model is suitability analysis, which follows six broad steps:

  • 1Define the goal
  • 2Identify criteria
  • 3Acquire and prepare the data
  • 4Transform each criterion to a common suitability scale
  • 5Weight and combine the criteria
  • 6Locate the most suitable sites

These steps are often shown in a flowchart because suitability analysis is really a sequence of spatial data inputs and GIS operations.

Step 1

Define the goal

The first step is to clearly define what problem the model is trying to solve. A good suitability analysis starts with a specific question. Examples:

  • ·Where is the best place to build a home?
  • ·Which land is most suitable for conservation?
  • ·Where should a new emergency shelter be located?
  • ·What areas are most suitable for solar development?

The goal matters because it shapes every later decision: which criteria matter, what data are needed, how suitability is defined, and how the final map is interpreted.

Step 2

Identify criteria

Once the goal is clear, the next step is to identify the criteria that will be used to evaluate each location. Two important types of criteria are used:

Factors

A factor is a criterion that increases or decreases the suitability of a location. Factors usually vary along a gradient. Examples: slope, distance to roads, land cost, soil drainage, solar radiation.

Constraints

A constraint is a criterion that limits where the activity can occur. Constraints usually act as exclusions. Examples: water bodies, protected areas, flood zones, parcels zoned against development, slopes above a certain threshold.

Example: home-site selection

For a home-site selection example, reasonable criteria might include: slope should not be too steep; southern aspects may be preferred for solar warming; soils should support septic systems; the site should be accessible to roads, but not too close for privacy reasons.

A strong suitability model does not just list criteria. It explains why each criterion matters and who it matters to.

Group brainstorm · work it out, then raise your hand

We’re siting a new emergency shelter. Name one factor (something that raises or lowers suitability by degree) and one constraint (something that rules an area out entirely). Work it out, then raise your hand.

Factors (gradient): distance to population centers, distance to major roads, elevation above the floodplain, distance from hazards.

Constraints (exclusion): inside a mapped flood zone, on protected/park land, on slopes above a safe threshold, on parcels not publicly owned. The test: a factor makes a place better or worse; a constraint makes it allowed or not.

Step 3

Acquire and prepare the data

After choosing the criteria, we must find and prepare the spatial data. This step may involve finding vector or raster data sources; projecting data into a common coordinate system; clipping data to the study area; matching raster resolution and extent; deriving new variables such as slope or aspect from elevation data; converting vector layers to raster when raster overlay will be used; and reclassifying categories into usable classes.

Step 4

Transform criteria to a common suitability scale

Because criteria are measured in different units, they must be transformed to a common scale before they can be combined. A common choice is a 0 to 1 scale, where 0 means not suitable and 1 means highly suitable. For example, slope may be measured in degrees, land cost in dollars, and distance to roads in meters — these cannot be added directly. They first need to be standardized.

Crisp (Boolean) membership

In a crisp or Boolean approach, a location is either in or out of the suitable set. Example: if distance from a lake is ≤ 0.5 km, assign 1; if greater than 0.5 km, assign 0.

This is simple and transparent, but it can be unrealistic because it creates abrupt cutoffs.

Fuzzy membership

In a fuzzy approach, locations can have partial membership in the suitable set. Suitability becomes a gradual measure rather than an all-or-nothing decision. Example: as distance from the lake increases, suitability decreases.

This often better matches real-world reasoning because many geographic boundaries are vague rather than sharp.

Step 5

Weight and combine criteria

After criteria are standardized, they can be weighted and combined. Weights represent the relative importance of each factor. If one factor matters more for the decision, it should contribute more strongly to the final suitability score.

Weighted linear combination
Suitability = (w1 × factor1) + (w2 × factor2) + … + (wn × factorn)

Constraints are usually applied afterward by masking or multiplying the factor-based suitability map so excluded areas become unavailable.

Try it · Weighted linear combination

One candidate site has three standardized factor scores (0–1). Move the weight sliders to change each factor’s importance, and watch the combined suitability update. Then flip the constraint to see it masked out.

Weighting methods

Several methods can be used to assign weights:

  • ·Equal weighting: each criterion gets the same weight. Simple and transparent, but it assumes all factors matter equally.
  • ·Rank ordering / rank sum: criteria are ranked from most to least important, and weights are derived from that ranking. Useful if you want to order criteria but do not want to make detailed pairwise judgments.
  • ·Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP): compares each criterion to every other criterion in terms of relative importance. These pairwise comparisons build a comparison matrix and derive weights.

AHP is especially useful because it is more structured and it lets us check whether the judgments are logically consistent.

AHP in plain language

Suppose we compare three criteria — proximity to roads, slope, and land cost. We ask questions like: how much more important is proximity to roads than slope? How much more important is land cost than proximity to roads? From these judgments, we build a pairwise comparison matrix, normalize it, and calculate the weights.

Step 6

Locate the most suitable sites

The final suitability surface can be interpreted in different ways depending on the project. You might identify the highest-value cells; classify the final surface into low, medium, and high suitability; select the top-ranked candidate sites; or apply additional filters such as parcel size, contiguity, or distance from competitors.

The overall workflow: vector analysis is slightly different

The key ideas are the same, just slightly simplified because we don’t have the advantage of representing the world continuously. Instead of a grid of standardized cells, vector suitability works with overlay of discrete features and their attributes.

Uncertainty in suitability analysis

Suitability analysis is powerful, but it is not objective truth.

Geographic representation is always a simplification of the real world, and uncertainty enters at every stage. Sources of uncertainty include how the problem is defined; how criteria are selected; how variables are measured; how categories are defined; how thresholds are chosen; how suitability is transformed; how weights are assigned; and the scale and zoning of the data.

Vagueness and ambiguity

Some criteria are uncertain because their meaning is vague or ambiguous. What counts as “urban”? What slope is “too steep”? What counts as “near” a road? What density qualifies as woodland? This is one reason fuzzy membership can be useful: it acknowledges that many spatial concepts do not have perfectly sharp boundaries.

How should we measure the coastline, which has no natural unit of analysis?

Error vs. uncertainty

It is useful to distinguish between error and uncertainty. Error is a measurable difference between a recorded value and a true value. Uncertainty is broader and includes vagueness, ambiguity, and incomplete knowledge.

Key takeaways

1
It makes trade-offs explicit. Suitability analysis turns multiple criteria and trade-offs into a structured, transparent GIS workflow.
2
The goal drives everything. A clear goal determines which criteria, data, transformations, and interpretations make sense.
3
Factors vs. constraints. Factors change suitability by degree; constraints exclude areas entirely.
4
Standardize before combining. Criteria must usually be put on a common scale before they can be combined, especially when measured in different units.
5
Results are not objective truth. Uncertainty enters through data choices, thresholds, weighting, scale, and vague concepts like “near” or “too steep.”
